To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the likelihood of cooperation is increasing (i) in the innovator’s control over intellectual property, (ii) in the presence of venture capital financing and (iii) in the relative cost advantage of the incumbent over the start-up innovator for control of specialized complementary inputs.
start-up innovators are more likely to challenge market structure if they have control over intellectual property and have lower bargaining costs.
start-up innovators are more likely to cooperate with established firms if they have a greater control over their intellectual property and if the costs to control complementary assets are high.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the conditions under which the gale of innovation and creative destruction are likely to be unleashed.

the question of how start-up innovators can be induced to cooperate with established firms in the absence of a market for ideas, and the conditions under which they will instead choose to compete with them.
how the commercialization strategy of a start-up innovator affects its impact on the product market structure and the pace of technological change.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, while start-up innovators can and do cooperate with incumbents, the conditions under which they do so are limited and the resulting benefits are likely to be small.
, when start-up firms have a high bargaining power and control of intellectual property rights, cooperation is more likely.
the more difficult it is for start-up innovators to protect and commercialize their ideas, the more likely they are to compete with incumbents.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the more start-ups can control their ideas, and the lower their transaction costs of bargaining, the more likely they are to cooperate with incumbents.

the market for ideas is imperfect, and that this imperfection is the key factor determining the extent to which start-up innovator strategies reinforce or challenge the market power of incumbent firms.
the propensity of start-up innovators to compete with incumbents in the product market is increasing in the relative cost and difficulty of appropriating returns to innovation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the commercialization strategy of start-ups is not exogenous to market conditions.
start-up innovators' commercialization strategies are endogenously determined by the market for ideas.
the commercialization of start-up innovation is likely to spur creative destruction in the product market when start-ups have the bargaining power to extract rents from their innovation.
